hypothesis: An adversary who compromised Windows hosts in this network stole credentials from them (MITRE ATT&CK tactic: Credential Access).

frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network harvested credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: Evidence of credential theft tooling or artifacts on Windows hosts, such as LSASS process memory access (e.g., procdump, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, Task Manager dump), Mimikatz/Sekurlsa module execution, SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM registry hive or NTDS.dit extraction, cached domain credential access, DPAPI master key or Credential Manager vault access, browser password store reads, or Kerberos ticket extraction (kirbi files, Rubeus/kerberoasting), correlated with suspicious process lineage or unauthorized access to those credential stores.
frame.what_would_refute: No credential-access artifacts or telemetry on any Windows host: no LSASS memory reads or dumps, no registry hive or NTDS.dit copies, no DPAPI/Credential Manager/browser credential store access, no Kerberos ticket extraction, and no credential-dumping tool execution or related file writes across the environment.

verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 verified malicious finding (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: The pivot confirms credential-access tooling: PsExec64 with cleartext credentials delivering a PyInstaller python.exe credential payload to nashua, plus Rar/sdelete packaging and wiping of collected secrets.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: Beyond the LSASS anchor, the PsExec-delivered PyInstaller python.exe on nashua (spawned by PSEXESVC.exe) unpacked credential-tooling DLLs and beaconed to 192.168.0.4:8443.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: lsass.exe set HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\F on scranton; no reg save/hive-copy command lines observed.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No ntds/ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow command lines, .dit file creation, or ntds object access in any dataset (C025-C031 zero hits).

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: No access to SECURITY\Policy\Secrets or lsadump references in security/powershell/other datasets (C035-C039 zero hits).

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: lsass.exe repeatedly set HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 on nashua during the attacker's active window; no direct SECURITY\Cache read captured.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: No DCSync indicators: no 4662 replication-rights access, no 4929/4930/4931, no drsuapi/lsadump/dcsync command lines (C047-C051 zero hits).

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: All packet-capture activity (netsh trace start/stop, logman ETW traces) on scranton.dmevals.local is spawned by the Azure Network Watcher agent (NetworkWatcherAgent.exe) and Azure Guest Agent (WaAppAgent.exe) as SYSTEM, i.e. legitimate platform telemetry. The PowerShell Add-Type hit is PowerShellGet module loading. No pktmon/npcap/winpcap/windump/rawcap drivers or capture scripts were found on any host, so no adversary network sniffing is observed.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: Masquerading cod.3aka3.scr in C:\ProgramData\victim accessed the LSA registry key and loaded GUI input DLLs (user32/gdi32/win32u/msctf), with outbound C2 to 192.168.0.5:1234.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: No keylogger artifacts found: no GetAsyncKeyState/SetWindowsHookEx/keylog strings in PowerShell, no Keyboard/Input registry object access. The .scr binary's GUI DLL loads are suggestive but no explicit keylogging evidence.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: No credential-prompt or GUI input capture commands (Get-Credential/prompt) observed in sysmon or security process creation events.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No web portal capture: no login/portal/vpn URLs in zeek HTTP, no matching file writes or process command lines.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: PowerShell.exe opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (full access) on scranton.dmevals.local, consistent with credential API hooking/credential access.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Only one credential-validation event (4776, AUDIT_SUCCESS Status 0x0) in the entire security window; zero 4625/4771 failures and no brute-force pattern.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: PowerShell 'password' matches are hardcoded secrets in credential-theft/exfil scripts (Get-PrivateKeys, Invoke-Exfil), not guessing loops; no failed logons.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: No cracking tooling (hashcat/Mimikatz/DumpCreds), no ntds.dit/SAM file writes; lsass/SAM access is dumping/OS behaviour, not offline cracking.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: No 4625/4771 failures and no spray scripts; 4648 targets are dominated by pbeesly and the single 4776 succeeded.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No failed logons, no login/auth process command lines, and no credential-stuffing scripts; only benign logon notifications observed.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA/smart-card/credential-provider interception artifacts. 4648 explicit-credential logons are PsExec lateral movement by pbeesly and routine winlogon/taskhostw localhost logons; the credential-referencing 4104 script is an exfiltration function (Invoke-Exfil) with hardcoded creds; lsass process-access is benign svchost 0x1000 queries plus a PowerShell-remoting wsmprovhost session; 'Credential' registry writes are Credential Guard / CredentialEnrollmentManager OS configuration.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local a PowerShell process dropped hostui.lnk into the StartUp folder (forced-auth trigger) and a masqueraded C:\Windows\System32\hostui.exe was launched via 'Start-Process ... -verb runas', then spawned PowerShell reading HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Javasoft piped to Invoke-Expression and a hidden base64 PowerShell. This is a forced-authentication/elevation chain consistent with T1187.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: PowerShell.exe on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (full access) at 03:05:16 UTC, in the same pbeesly session that ran Get-PrivateKeys, Get-Clipboard and privilege-enumeration script blocks — consistent with exploitation/abuse for credential access.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: No access to browser cookie/login databases was found. PowerShell 4104 'Cookies' matches are benign DSC module helper scripts (CommonResourceHelper.psm1); Sysmon file-create 'cookie/session' hits are OS artifacts (INetCookies cache, .etl session files) from svchost.exe/System; no 4663 object access to any browser cookie store; only normal MicrosoftEdge process launches. The malicious PowerShell on scranton.dmevals.local is screen-capture/keystroke/exfil activity, not web session cookie theft.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: Umbrella technique: confirmed credential theft activity on scranton.dmevals.local by user pbeesly (private key export, plaintext password in PsExec command line).

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: pbeesly's cleartext password Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by was passed on the PsExec64.exe command line from scranton to NASHUA, and a password-protected Rar archive of *pass*/*login*/*admin*/*vpn* files was created on nashua.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: All credential-path registry writes were by legitimate system processes (svchost/winlogon/wininit/services); no reg query/save of credential hives.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No ConsoleHost_history/PSReadLine access or shell-history reads found in any dataset.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Get-PrivateKeys exported all LocalMachine certificates to .pfx files on scranton, confirmed by Sysmon file creation, then cleaned up.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: SYSVOL/GptTmpl.inf writes were normal Group Policy processing by svchost.exe; no GPP cpassword collection observed.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: PowerShell 'Screenshot' background job capturing the user session to Downloads and download of 7Zip4Powershell packaging module on scranton; consistent with credential/session collection but no direct credential-store read observed.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: All browser credential-store checks (C193-C198) returned zero hits; no Login Data/logins.json/browser process access seen.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: No vault/Credential Manager file or registry access (C201, C202 zero hits); LSASS handle access is benign svchost/Azure/system processes.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: No 1Password/KeePass/LastPass file, command-line or script-block artifacts (C206-C208 zero hits).

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: LSASS handle accesses are dominated by legitimate system/security processes (svchost 289, AntimalwareConfig, Azure telemetry) with query-limited masks (0x1000/0x1400); rare high-mask accesses from PowerShell/wsmprovhost show benign ntdll/KERNELBASE and PowerShell Management call traces. No authentication process modification.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: 4624 logons are routine machine-account (NEWYORK$) network logons (Type 3) from local/link-local addresses; no DC authentication backdoor or 4648 explicit-credential abuse.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No password filter DLL registration, System32 DLL drops, or Notification Packages/PasswordFilter references found.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No 4739 events, Set-ADUser/ReversibleEncryption command lines, or reversible-encryption strings found.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739/4738/4732 events or authentication-policy PowerShell activity found.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No 5136/5137/5141 directory change events or adfs/azuread references found.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No System32/SysWOW64 DLL writes or 4657/4656 registry/object access found.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: SMB/LDAP/Kerberos connections (383 sysmon events) all originate from legitimate Windows components (lsass, ADWS, dfsrs, svchost) to the DC 10.0.0.4; no adversary-in-the-middle positioning seen.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: DNS resolutions are correct (NASHUA->10.0.1.6, NEWYORK->10.0.0.4, SCRANTON->10.0.1.4); no LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning. Service installs are PSEXESVC (PsExec) and javamtsup, not relay tooling.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: arp.exe /a and netsh trace are spawned by Azure platform agents (WindowsAzureGuestAgent, NetworkWatcherAgent, WindowsAzureTelemetryService, WaAppAgent) as SYSTEM; Zeek MAC-to-IP mapping is consistent, no MAC claiming multiple IPs.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP event codes, no dhcp command lines, no DHCP PowerShell, and no Zeek UDP traffic on ports 67/68 in any dataset.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: PowerShell.exe PID 2976 (the hidden stego-loader run by pbeesly on scranton) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF, full-access LSASS reads consistent with Kerberos ticket/credential theft.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: No krbtgt/DCSync/forged-ticket artifacts; Kerberos traffic is normal AES256 AS/TGS for pbeesly.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: No silver-ticket/Rubeus artifacts; TGS requests are legitimate service tickets for pbeesly.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: No Kerberoast/SPN/Invoke-Kerberoast artifacts; no RC4 downgrade in TGS requests.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: No AS-REP roast artifacts; AS exchanges show pre-authentication enabled (KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED then success).

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: A .scr payload in C:\ProgramData\victim and a PowerShell IEX stager decoding monkey.png were observed on scranton.dmevals.local, providing the execution context for the credential-theft toolchain, but no direct web-credential forgery artifact was seen.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: Only benign svchost.exe creation of a service-profile INetCookies file; no browser cookie theft, cookie manipulation, or SetCookie script blocks were found.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exported all LocalMachine certificates to password-protected .pfx files on scranton.dmevals.local, the classic precursor to stealing an ADFS token-signing certificate for SAML token forgery, followed by exfiltration and cleanup functions.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: 5 planned checks, all with zero hits

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran the PowerShell function Get-PrivateKeys (from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) which recursively enumerates cert:\LocalMachine and exports every certificate with a private key to $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\<random>.pfx using the hardcoded password 'saribas'; Sysmon event 11 confirms the created file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx from powershell.exe PID 3876. This is bulk theft of authentication certificates/private keys (T1649).

checks.purpose: Look for PowerShell that disables or modifies MFA-related AD attributes (Set-ADUser / Set-ADAuthenticationPolicy).
EventCode 4739 records domain policy changes, which is where MFA/authentication policy modifications would surface.
Check the 'other' channel for account/policy change events that could reflect MFA attribute tampering.

args.query: event.code:1 AND (process.command_line:*ADUser* OR process.command_line:*AuthenticationPolicy* OR process.command_line:*dsmod* OR process.command_line:*dsacls*)

checks.purpose: Stack processes whose command lines touch AD user/authentication policy objects.
Directory Service Changes (5136) capture modification of AD objects, including hybrid-identity/authentication-related attributes.

args.query: event.code:7 AND (win.ImageLoaded:*AAD* OR win.ImageLoaded:*Azure* OR win.ImageLoaded:*ADFS* OR win.ImageLoaded:*Identity*)

checks.purpose: Stack image loads of cloud/hybrid identity components that could indicate backdooring of the hybrid auth path.

args.query: FROM logs-windows.powershell-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE TO_LOWER(powershell.script_block_text) LIKE "*adfs*" OR TO_LOWER(powershell.script_block_text) LIKE "*azuread*" OR TO_LOWER(powershell.script_block_text) LIKE "*connect-msolservice*" OR TO_LOWER(powershell.script_block_text) LIKE "*new-azuread*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, powershell.script_block_text, _id, _index

checks.purpose: Find PowerShell touching ADFS/Azure AD hybrid identity configuration.
Check the 'other' channel for directory object create/delete/modify events tied to hybrid identity objects.

args.query: event.code:13 AND (win.TargetObject:*NetworkProvider* OR win.TargetObject:*Credential Provider* OR win.TargetObject:*Winlogon*)

checks.purpose: Stack registry modifications to NetworkProvider/Credential Provider/Winlogon keys where a malicious network provider DLL would be registered.
Stack loaded network-provider DLLs to spot non-standard ones loaded into authentication processes.
Look for newly written DLLs in system directories that could be dropped network provider DLLs.
Registry value modification events (4657) can capture creation of a NetworkProvider registry entry.
Check the 'other' channel for registry handle/value modification events related to provider registration.

args.query: event.code:3 AND (destination.port:445 OR destination.port:139 OR destination.port:389 OR destination.port:88)

checks.purpose: Stack network destinations for SMB/LDAP/Kerberos connections that could indicate relay or AiTM positioning.
Stack DNS queries to spot name-resolution anomalies consistent with poisoning.
Object access/permission-change events (4663/4670/4656) that ATT&CK associates with AiTM activity.
Check the 'other' channel for the same object-access events.
Stack Zeek connection/DNS/SMB activity to look for abnormal SMB authentication or name-resolution flows.

args.query: event.action:conn AND (destination.port:5355 OR destination.port:137 OR destination.port:445)

checks.purpose: Stack LLMNR/NBT-NS/SMB ports to find unusual responses or SMB authentication flows consistent with poisoning/relay.
Inspect SMB mapping/file and DCE-RPC activity that could reflect relayed authentication.

args.query: FROM logs-windows.powershell-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE TO_LOWER(powershell.script_block_text) LIKE "*enablemulticast*" OR TO_LOWER(powershell.script_block_text) LIKE "*llmnr*" OR TO_LOWER(powershell.script_block_text) LIKE "*responder*" OR TO_LOWER(powershell.script_block_text) LIKE "*inveigh*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, powershell.script_block_text, _id, _index

checks.purpose: Find PowerShell that disables LLMNR or references poisoning/relay tooling.
Stack SMB destinations to detect traffic redirected through a poisoned ARP path.
Stack DNS queries for anomalies accompanying ARP cache poisoning.
Filtering Platform connection/bind events (5156/5158) can reveal unexpected local network bindings from poisoning tools.
Check the 'other' channel for the same network connection/bind events.
Stack source MAC addresses to spot a single MAC claiming multiple IPs, a hallmark of ARP poisoning.

args.query: event.code:1341 OR event.code:1342 OR event.code:1020 OR event.code:1063

checks.purpose: DHCP server/address conflict and network config change events (1341/1342/1020/1063) that would indicate a rogue DHCP server or DHCP parameters being overridden on the host.
Stack all System-channel event codes to see whether any DHCP-related codes exist at all in this dataset before reading individual events.
PowerShell DHCP server configuration/rogue DHCP setup scripts (e.g. Install-WindowsFeature DHCP, Add-DhcpServerv4Scope) that would accompany DHCP spoofing.
Process creation of DHCP server administration tooling (netsh dhcp, Add-DhcpServerv4Scope) on Windows hosts.
Sysmon process creation showing DHCP server tooling or netsh dhcp commands used to stand up a rogue DHCP service.

args.query: event.action:conn AND network.transport:udp AND (destination.port:67 OR destination.port:68 OR source.port:67 OR source.port:68)

checks.purpose: DHCP (UDP 67/68) network flows in the Zeek window that could reveal an unauthorized DHCP server offering addresses.
Any process-access (Sysmon 10) or process-creation (Sysmon 1) records forwarded into windows.other that could show LSASS access for ticket theft.

findings.title: Credential-access tooling staged and executed by pbeesly across scranton and nashua
findings.summary: The credential-access activity is part of a broader intrusion by user pbeesly. On scranton.dmevals.local, pbeesly ran Sysinternals PsExec64.exe with cleartext credentials ('-u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by') to launch C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on \\NASHUA (03:11:18, 03:12:25, 03:13:28, 03:14:42), and used sdelete64.exe to wipe artifacts (e.g. C:\programdata\victim\???cod.3aka3.scr, C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Roaming\Draft.Zip). On nashua, C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe was spawned by C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe repeatedly (03:11:40-03:15:04), matching the lsass cached-credential registry writes. This establishes the actor and tooling behind the LSASS/SAM/cached-credential access.

findings.title: PowerShell opened LSASS with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS and read its memory on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, C:\windows\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and 0x1f3fff at 2020-05-02T03:05:16, with a call trace ending in an UNKNOWN module (C:\windows\SYSTEM32\ntdll.dll+9c584|C:\Windows\System32\KERNELBASE.dll+2732e|UNKNOWN(000001996D28200D)), indicating injected/reflective code rather than a signed tool. Windows Security 4663 corroborates the same second: user pbeesly's powershell.exe performed 'Read from process memory' (Access Mask 0x10) on \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe. PowerShell 4104 script blocks from pbeesly at 03:21:29 contain a reflective loader (GetProcAddress via Microsoft.Win32.UnsafeNativeMethods, VirtualAlloc/CreateThread pattern) and a base64 gzip-encoded hidden powershell payload, consistent with an in-memory credential-dumping toolchain. This is LSASS memory access for credential theft.

findings.title: PsExec-delivered python.exe (PyInstaller) executed on nashua via PSEXESVC and connected out to 192.168.0.4:8443
findings.summary: On nashua.dmevals.local, C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe (created by services.exe) spawned C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe as pbeesly at 03:11:40, 03:12:46, 03:13:49 and 03:15:03 UTC. The python.exe unpacked a PyInstaller bundle into C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Local\Temp\_MEI29522 (python27.dll, _ctypes.pyd, _ssl.pyd, pywintypes27.dll, win32pipe.pyd etc.) and then opened many outbound connections to 192.168.0.4:8443. This is the credential-access payload the anchors' tooling staged; it is not covered by the LSASS/SAM/cache anchors.

findings.title: Masquerading .scr binary in C:\ProgramData\victim accesses LSA registry and loads GUI input DLLs
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly launched C:\ProgramData\victim\cod.3aka3.scr (command line "C:\ProgramData\victim\cod.3aka3.scr" /S) at 2020-05-02T02:55:56Z. The binary has no version/company/original-filename metadata, masquerades as a screen saver, loaded GUI/input-related DLLs (user32.dll, gdi32.dll, win32u.dll, msctf.dll), opened \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Control\Lsa with Query key value access, and made an outbound TCP connection to 192.168.0.5:1234. This is consistent with input capture / credential API hooking activity.

findings.title: PowerShell.exe opened LSASS with full access (0x1FFFFF) on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z, C:\windows\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS), the access level used to read/hook credential material in LSASS. A second access with 0x1F3FFF was also recorded. This is consistent with credential API hooking / LSASS credential access.

On scranton.dmevals.local, powershell.exe (PID 3876, running as SYSTEM) created C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\StartUp\hostui.lnk at 2020-05-02T03:04:23Z. A shortcut placed in the StartUp folder is a classic T1187 forced-authentication trigger: when the user logs on and the .lnk is resolved/opened it can cause the host to authenticate outbound (SMB/WebDAV) to an attacker-controlled target, leaking NTLM credentials. The same PowerShell session had earlier written hostui.txt into C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\SysinternalsSuite\, indicating the attacker staged the hostui payload.

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, powershell.exe ran 'Start-Process C:\Windows\System32\hostui.exe -verb runas' (2020-05-02T03:21:19Z), spawning C:\Windows\System32\hostui.exe (PID 8452) at High integrity as DMEVALS\pbeesly. The binary masquerades as a Windows component (Company, Description, Product, OriginalFileName all '-') yet sits in System32. hostui.exe then spawned powershell.exe reading 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Javasoft' 'value Supplement' piped to Invoke-Expression, which in turn launched a hidden base64-encoded PowerShell (-nop -w hidden -e ...). This is the forced-authentication/execution chain: a fake System32 binary coerced into elevation that then executes attacker code.

findings.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exports all LocalMachine certificates to .pfx on scranton.dmevals.local
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02T03:04:56Z (host local 2020-05-01 23:04:56) on scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly executed a PowerShell function 'Get-PrivateKeys' loaded from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1 (PID 3876). The script enumerates cert:\LocalMachine recursively and, for every certificate with a Thumbprint, calls Export-PfxCertificate to write $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\<random>.pfx protected by the hardcoded plaintext password 'saribas'. Sysmon event 11 confirms the resulting file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx created by C:\windows\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe (PID 3876) one second later. This is bulk theft of authentication certificates/private keys from the machine certificate store, matching T1649 (Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates). The script name, hardcoded password and mass-export loop are not normal administrative behaviour.

findings.title: lsass.exe wrote the SAM account hive value on scranton

This is the SAM account database value; the write occurred seconds after lsass.exe was (re)started at 03:19:09.809. findings.summary: No Kerberoasting activity was found: PowerShell script-block searches for 'kerberoast'/'SPN'/'Invoke-Kerberoast' returned zero hits (C287), and the zeek Kerberos TGS requests are limited to a small set of normal services for pbeesly with AES256 encryption (no RC4/etype 23 downgrade typical of roasting).

findings.title: No AS-REP Roasting evidence observed
findings.summary: No AS-REP roasting was found: PowerShell script-block searches for 'asrep'/'AS-REP'/'GetNPUsers' returned zero hits (C295) and sysmon process-creation searches for asrep/GetNPUsers/rubeus command lines returned zero hits (C298). The zeek AS exchanges for pbeesly all show KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED followed by a successful pre-authenticated AS-REP, i.e. pre-authentication is enabled — the opposite of an AS-REP-roastable account.

The only cookie-related file event was a single creation of C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\AppData\Local\Packages\warp_jit_db4a1097-b484-4973-bbf2-a04208ecd4d4\AC\INetCookies by svchost.exe on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:21:05, which is normal Windows service-profile cookie-store activity, not browser cookie theft or forging. No PowerShell script blocks referencing cookies/SetCookie were found, and no security-log access to Cookies or Login Data objects was observed.
findings.title: No web-cookie theft or forgery observed
Certificate store registry value change on nashua.dmevals.local is Sysmon self-monitoring
findings.summary: The only 4657 registry modification touching the certificate store was on nashua.dmevals.local at 2020-05-01T23:16:19-04:00, changing a value under \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\ROOT\Certificates\BE36A4562FB2EE05DBB3D32323ADF445084ED656. The modifying process is C:\Windows\Sysmon.exe and the account is the machine account NASHUA$, i.e. Sysmon's own certificate-store monitoring, not an adversary importing a forged authentication certificate. No corresponding certificate file creation or PowerShell certificate manipulation was seen on nashua.

findings.title: Kerberos TGT requests (4768) show no certificate-based authentication anomaly
findings.summary: All 14 Kerberos TGT requests (event 4768) in the window were on newyork.dmevals.local and belong to two accounts: the interactive user pbeesly (9 requests, S-1-5-21-1830255721-3727074217-2423397540-1107) and the machine account SCRANTON$ (5 requests). All request the krbtgt service with normal client addresses (10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6) and standard realm names; no PKINIT/certificate-based or otherwise anomalous TGT issuance is visible, so these are routine domain logons rather than evidence of forged authentication certificates.
